newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Sterling rally falters on modest rate rise.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Sterling rally falters on modest rate rise.

text.p: A modest 1/4-point rise in British interest rates on Thursday took the steam out of sterling's rally, but analysts said the pound's rise to three German marks may only have been interrupted briefly.
In shares, retailers rallied on a belief that the consumer boom would continue at least for the time being and the overall market ended slightly higher on the day.
Government bond prices shrugged off the increase in the cost of credit, ending the day virtually unchanged.
The Bank of England's monetary tightening led to a roller-coaster session in foreign exchange dealing rooms.
The pound initially dropped a pfennig on disappointment that the newly-independent Bank's monetary policy committee had not plumped for a tougher 1/2-point increase in base rates to seven percent.
Prospects of further interest-rate increases sent the pound back up to near six-year highs on the mark but it ended the European session close to its lows for the day of 2.95 marks.
Earlier this week sterling hit a six-year high of 2.9760 marks after last week's budget, which was not seen as being enough to rein in a booming consumer sector.

While some in the market saw sterling topping out for a while, one trader at a U.S. bank said, "The market is still mainly bullish for a rise above three marks and dealers are keen to buy it back at lower levels."
Citibank's chief economist Neil MacKinnon added, "Sterling is well supported by the interest-rate rise and investors are looking for further gains."

"Nothing has happened that could take the shine off sterling," said David Bloom, currency strategist at HSBC James Capel. "It will contiue to be driven higher by favourable interest rate differentials."
The FTSE 100 index of blue-chip shares ended 5.4 points higher at 4,767.8, near the day's best level. However, expectations of further rate rises capped gains.
"The perception is that (a 25 basis point rise) is not enough and therefore we have more rate rises to look forward to," said Nomura stock strategist Nick Knight.
There was a sense or relief on the market that the Bank of England had held back at least for now.

An immediate 1/2-point hammer blow from the monetary policy committee could have sent sterling shooting up even more strongly, putting further pressure on exporters already reeling from an 18 percent rise in the pound in just under one year.

Retailers benefited most in Thursday's market, with stores group Kingfisher initially leading the rally. At one stage Kingfisher was up nearly seven percent at 739, before it settled at 703-1/2, up 11 pence on the day.
Electrical retailer Dixons, already on a roll on the back of strong trading figures out on Wednesday, closed 17-1/2 pence higher at 554.

On the government bond market there was a mixed reaction. The September gilts future initially jumped on the so-called relief factor, but the market then backtracked on prospects of further rate rises.
The September gilt future settled just 2/32 lower at 114-07/32.
